entry: Group of venomous snakes endemic to [[Asia]]. Its record length of 5.85 m (19.2 ft) makes it the world's longest venomous snake. Taxonomic revision now treats the king cobra as a species complex rather than a single species. It chiefly hunts other snakes, and it is the only snake that builds an above-ground nest for its eggs, which the female guards. Its [[Venom|venom]] can cause rapid neurotoxic and cytotoxic symptoms that require prompt antivenom. Aggression toward humans usually arises only when an individual is cornered or inadvertently exposes itself. Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and regarded as the national reptile of [[India]].

Ancient kingdom of the Horn of Africa and South Arabia, based in present-day Eritrea and northern [[Ethiopia]]. Emerging from the earlier Dʿmt civilization, it was founded in the 1st century, and its capital was the city of Axum. It became a major power on the trade route between Rome and India and gained a monopoly of Indian Ocean trade. Under Ezana (320s–c. 360) it adopted [[Christianity]] as its state religion, and it conquered [[Meroë]] for a short period. Under Kaleb (514–542) it invaded Himyar in Yemen, and its territory reached around 2,500,000 sq km (970,000 sq mi), though this was later lost in the Aksumite–Persian wars. Its decline began by the 7th century, when it ceased to mint currency, and the kingdom collapsed under uncertain circumstances around 960.

Medieval and early modern kingdom on the [[Iberian Peninsula]], in what is now Aragon, Spain. It originated as a county around Jaca and gained independence under Ramiro I, its first de facto king, after the 1035 division of the Kingdom of Pamplona. Expansion into [[Al-Andalus]] moved the capital to Huesca in 1096 and to Zaragoza in 1118. The marriage of Queen Petronilla to the Count of Barcelona created the Crown of Aragon, which later included Catalonia, Valencia, Majorca, Sicily, Naples and Sardinia. In 1479 the crowns of Aragon and Castile were united, forming the nucleus of modern Spain. The kingdom kept its own *Corts* until the *Nueva Planta* decrees of 1707–1715 by Philip V centralized power in Spain.

Ancient kingdom of the Near East, existing from 189 BC to 428 AD. Its origins lay in an Achaemenid satrapy formed from [[Urartu]], and the Artaxiad dynasty took the throne in 189 BC. Under [[Tigranes the Great]] the kingdom reached its peak from 83 to 69 BC, reincorporating Sophene and conquering much of the falling [[Seleucid Empire]] before Rome conquered it in 69 BC. Rome and Parthia then contested Armenia, and the Arsacid dynasty was founded in 52. From 114 to 118 it was a province of the [[Roman Empire]] under [[Trajan]]. Under Tiridates III, Armenia became the first state to adopt Christianity as its state religion. In 387 the kingdom was partitioned between Byzantine and Persian Armenia, and its last Arsacid king was deposed in 428.

Medieval and early modern monarchy in Central Europe, predecessor of the modern [[Czech Republic]]. Its duchy was raised to a kingdom in 1198 by Přemysl Ottokar I, and the status was recognized in 1212 by a Golden Bull of Sicily issued by Emperor Frederick II. Its kings were prince-electors of the [[Holy Roman Empire]], and the crown also ruled at various times Moravia, Silesia and Lusatia. The [[House of Habsburg]] held the throne from 1526, and Prague was the imperial seat in the late 14th century. Bohemia became part of the Habsburg Austrian Empire in 1806 and of Austria-Hungary from 1867, remaining a separate kingdom until 1918. After World War I the kingdom was dissolved, and Bohemia became the core of [[Czechoslovakia]].

Medieval Christian kingdom on the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. It originated as a 9th-century county on the eastern frontier of the Kingdom of León and became a separate kingdom in 1065. It was again united with León from 1072 to 1157, and after 1230 the union became permanent. Castilian kings conquered much of southern Iberia from Islamic principalities, taking Toledo in 1085 and Seville in 1248. The marriage of [[Isabella I of Castile]] and [[Ferdinand II of Aragon]] in 1469 forged a dynastic union, and the 1492 conquest of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada completed the [[Reconquista]]. Castile and León, with their southern acquisitions, came to be known as the Crown of Castile, a term that also encompassed overseas expansion.

Sovereign state on the island of Great Britain, from 927 to 1707. In 927 [[Æthelstan]] united the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and conquered York, the last Viking kingdom. The [[Norman Conquest]] of 1066 moved the capital to Westminster. [[Edward I]] completed the conquest of Wales in 1284. Under [[Edward III]] the English Parliament developed, and the kingdom became a formidable military power. After the [[Hundred Years' War]] and the Wars of the Roses, it held no continental land except Calais. The Tudors extended royal power, and [[Henry VIII]] oversaw the English Reformation. Accession of [[James VI and I]] in 1603 created the Union of the Crowns, and colonization of Virginia began in 1607. Civil war ended with the execution of Charles I in 1649, and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 established that monarchs could not govern without Parliament's consent. In 1707 England and Scotland were united as the [[Kingdom of Great Britain]].

Monarchy of Western Europe, descended from the western Frankish realm of the [[Carolingian Empire]]. Ceded to Charles the Bald under the Treaty of Verdun (843), the realm passed to the [[Capetian dynasty]] when Hugh Capet was elected king in 987. The first king to style himself King of France was Philip II, in 1190. Medieval France was a decentralized feudal monarchy, and its rivalry with the [[House of Plantagenet]] led to the [[Hundred Years' War]] (1337–1453). In the early modern era the monarchy became absolute, most notably under [[Louis XIV]]. Religious conflict with the [[Huguenots]] produced the Wars of Religion (1562–1598). At its peak in 1680, the French colonial empire covered over 10 million sq km (3.9 million sq mi), second only to the [[Spanish Empire]]. The monarchy was abolished in 1792 during the French Revolution and restored in 1814.

Medieval state in [[Eastern Europe]], existing from 1199 to 1349. Its territory lay mostly in modern Ukraine, with parts of Belarus, Poland, Romania, Moldova and Lithuania. Roman the Great united the principalities of Galicia and Volhynia at the turn of the 13th century. After the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus' (1239–1241), Prince [[Daniel of Galicia]] pledged allegiance to [[Batu Khan]] of the [[Golden Horde]] in 1246. In 1253 he was crowned king of Ruthenia by the [[Pope]] in an attempt to form an anti-Mongol alliance, but efforts to free the kingdom from Golden Horde influence failed. Poland conquered Galicia in 1349, and its king, [[Casimir III the Great]], took the title King of Poland and Ruthenia. Volhynia came under the [[Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] and became a Lithuanian province in 1452.

Medieval kingdom that formed the original core of the [[Holy Roman Empire]]. It evolved from the eastern Frankish kingdom created by the Treaty of Verdun in 843. Its core consisted of the stem duchies of Saxony, Franconia, Thuringia, Bavaria and Swabia, and in the 10th century it consolidated Lotharingia. From 962 its kings claimed the imperial title. The kingdom eventually encompassed present-day Germany, Austria, Slovenia, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, as well as parts of Switzerland, Belgium, France and Poland. It had no single official name, and the name Germany did not appear in official royal titles until 1508. From the late 11th century, during the Investiture Contest, its kings adopted the title *rex Romanorum* (king of the Romans).

Sovereign state in Western Europe, created by the Acts of Union 1707 from [[Kingdom of England|England]] and Scotland. It had a single parliament at the Palace of Westminster, while English and Scots law remained separate. Hanoverian monarchs ruled from 1714. Victory in the [[Seven Years' War]] gave Britain dominance in India through the [[East India Company]] and in North America, but it lost the [[Thirteen Colonies]] in the [[American Revolutionary War]]. Jacobite risings ended in defeat in 1746. On 1 January 1801 the kingdom merged into the [[United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland]].

Central European monarchy that existed from 1000 to 1946. Stephen I was crowned at Esztergom around 1000, and the Árpád dynasty led the kingdom for about 300 years. The kingdom became a European power in the 12th century. Ottoman occupation of its central and southern territories in the 16th century partitioned it into three parts. The [[House of Habsburg]] held the throne from the Battle of Mohács in 1526 until 1918. Under [[Matthias Corvinus]] the kingdom flourished, and [[John Hunyadi]] won victories over the Ottomans in the 15th century. From 1867 it was part of Austria-Hungary. The monarchy ended with the deposition of Charles IV in 1918, and the Treaty of Trianon removed 72% of Hungary's territory.

Ancient Georgian kingdom of Kartli, called Iberia in Greco-Roman geography. Its population, the Iberians, formed the nucleus of the Kartvelians, or Georgians, and Mtskheta was its capital. According to Georgian tradition, Pharnavaz became the first king around 302 BC, though the medieval chronicles are considered semi-legendary. Iberia was either an independent state or a dependent of larger empires, notably the Sassanid and [[Roman Empire|Roman]] empires. In the 4th century, under King Mirian III, [[Christianity]] became the state religion. In 580 Hormizd IV abolished the monarchy after the death of Bakur III, and Iberia became a Persian province ruled by a marzpan. Iberia, together with Colchis to its west, formed the nucleus of the unified medieval Kingdom of Georgia under the Bagrationi dynasty.

Unitary monarchy in Southern Europe, proclaimed in 1861 and abolished in 1946. Victor Emmanuel II of Sardinia was proclaimed king of Italy after the Risorgimento unified several states. Italy gained Veneto in 1866 and took Rome in 1870, ending papal temporal power. It entered [[World War I]] on the Allied side in 1915. In 1922 [[Benito Mussolini]] became prime minister, and the Fascist regime invaded Ethiopia in 1935 in the [[Second Italo-Ethiopian War]]. Italy joined [[World War II]] on the Axis side in 1940. After the Fascist regime fell in 1943, a referendum in 1946 abolished the monarchy.

Crusader state in the [[Levant]], established after the [[First Crusade]]. Godfrey of Bouillon's accession in 1099 began a kingdom that lasted until the fall of Acre in 1291. After the siege of Jerusalem in 1187, [[Saladin]]'s Ayyubid Sultanate overran almost all of it, and the kingdom was re-established at Acre after the [[Third Crusade]] in 1192. Its rulers and elite were predominantly French, and the Italian maritime republics of Venice and Genoa grew increasingly influential through naval support. At its height in the mid-12th century, it covered roughly modern Israel, Palestine and southern Lebanon, including [[Beirut]].

Central African kingdom, c. 1390–1914, in present-day northern [[Angola]], western [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], southern Gabon and the [[Republic of the Congo]]. It was founded around 1390 through a political [[Marriage]] between two KiKongo-speaking peoples. Its rulers were called Manikongo, the Portuguese form of Mwene Kongo, and its capital was M'banza-Kongo, formerly São Salvador. King Nzinga a Nkuwu converted to [[Christianity]] in 1491, taking the name João I. Under his successor Afonso I (r. 1509–1543), the kingdom deepened its ties with Portugal, though it later supplied war captives to the transatlantic slave trade. It was an independent state until 1862, then intermittently a Portuguese vassal. After a Kongo revolt in 1914, Portugal abolished the titular monarchy, which was restored as an honorific from 1915 to 1975.

Ancient kingdom in [[Nubia]], centered on the [[Nile]] Valley in present-day northern [[Sudan]] and southern [[Egypt]]. The city-state of Kerma dominated the Nile Valley between 2450 and 1450 BC, and Egypt ruled much of Nubia during the New Kingdom. Kashta became king of Upper Egypt in the 8th century BC, and his successor Piye established the Kushite-ruled Twenty-fifth Dynasty. Kushite monarchs ruled Egypt for over a century until the Assyrian conquest in the mid-7th century BC. The capital then moved to [[Meroë]]. Kush weakened in the 4th century AD amid climatic decline, rebellions and invasions by the Noba. After the Aksumites captured Meroë, the kingdom split into Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia. Its people had their own language and script, and they were known for mastering [[Archery]].

German state, existing from 1701 to 1918, with its capital at [[Berlin]]. It took its name from the historical region of Prussia and was ruled by the Hohenzollern dynasty from the Margraviate of Brandenburg. Under [[Frederick the Great]] it became a European great power, fighting the [[Seven Years' War]] against Austria, Russia, France and Sweden. Prussia drove the formation of the North German Confederation after the [[Austro-Prussian War]] of 1866. Following the [[Franco-Prussian War]] of 1870–1871, the [[German Empire]] unified most German states under Prussian hegemony. The German Revolution of 1918–1919 transformed the kingdom into the Free State of Prussia, which was abolished in 1947.

State in southern Italy, existing from 1130 to 1816. Its founder, [[Roger II of Sicily]], was proclaimed king on Christmas Day 1130. The [[Normans]] had conquered Sicily from its Muslim rulers, and the island was under Norman control by 1091. Roger II united the lands he inherited, including the Duchy of Apulia and the County of Sicily. After the Sicilian Vespers revolt of 1282 freed the island from Angevin rule, the mainland remained under the Angevins as a separate kingdom, informally called Naples. The island became part of the Crown of Aragon in 1412, and Spanish control strengthened after the dynastic union of Castile and Aragon. Following the [[Napoleon|Napoleonic]] period, it was merged with Naples to form the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, which became part of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

Sovereign state of Northwestern Europe and the Caribbean, united under the Dutch monarch. Its four constituent countries are [[Aruba]], [[Curaçao]], the Netherlands and [[Sint Maarten]]. The European Netherlands comprises roughly 98% of the kingdom's land area and population, and Bonaire, Saba and Sint Eustatius are special municipalities in the Caribbean. The kingdom emerged after the defeat of [[Napoleon]], when William Frederick, Prince of Orange, became King William I in 1815. In 1830 the southern provinces seceded as [[Belgium]], a separation recognized in 1839. That year Luxembourg also left the kingdom, continuing as a grand duchy in personal union with the Dutch monarch until 1890.

Taxonomic rank immediately below [[Domain (taxonomy)|domain]] and above [[Phylum|phylum]]. Carl Linnaeus introduced rank-based nomenclature in 1735 and recognized two kingdoms of living things, animal and plant, and he placed minerals in a third. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's observations of microscopic organisms led to new schemes, and in 1866 [[Ernst Haeckel]] proposed a third kingdom of life, the Protista. Textbooks in the United States have traditionally used six kingdoms, while those in India and the United Kingdom, among other countries, used five. Domain was introduced above kingdom in 1990. Some recent classifications have abandoned the term because some traditional kingdoms are not monophyletic.

Family of small to medium-sized, brightly colored birds (Alcedinidae) in the order Coraciiformes. Kingfishers have large heads, long pointed bills and short legs. Most species live in tropical regions of Africa, Asia and Oceania, but the family is also found in Europe and the Americas. Most kingfishers live in forests, but some live far from water and eat small invertebrates. Most species nest in tunnels dug into banks. The family is divided into three subfamilies and 19 genera. Fossil kingfishers are known from Lower Eocene rocks in [[Wyoming]]. The scientific name derives from the Greek *halkyon*, linked to a myth in which the gods revived the drowned Alcyone and Ceyx as kingfishers.

Capital and chief port of [[Jamaica]], on the island's southeastern coast. The city faces a natural harbor protected by the Palisadoes, a long sand spit. Kingston was founded on 22 July 1692, shortly after an earthquake destroyed nearby Port Royal, and by 1716 it had become the largest town and trade center of Jamaica. The city's central districts are the historic Downtown and New Kingston. It is the largest English-speaking city south of the [[United States]] in the Western Hemisphere. Its music, including [[Reggae|reggae]], ska and dancehall, grew out of local sound systems. The harbor handles over 90% of the island's cargo.

Port city in the East Riding of Yorkshire, England, on the River Hull (pop., 2025: 273,257). Known as Yorkshire's maritime city, it was founded as a port in the late 12th century by the monks of Meaux Abbey to export wool. It was renamed Kingston upon Hull in 1299. Hull was an early battleground of the [[English Civil War]]. Its 18th-century Member of Parliament, [[William Wilberforce]], took a prominent part in the abolition of the slave trade in Britain. Hull was UK City of Culture in 2017 and has been ranked among the most deprived cities in the country.

Nocturnal, tree-dwelling [[Mammal|mammal]] of the family [[Procyonidae]], native to [[Tropical rainforest|tropical rainforests]] from Mexico through Central and South America. It is the only member of the genus *Potos*, and it is also known as the honey bear. It is related to [[Coati|coatis]] and [[Raccoon|raccoons]]. Mostly frugivorous, it is hunted for the pet trade, for its skin, which is used for wallets and saddles, and for its meat. Honduras included the species in Appendix III of CITES. Kinkajous may live up to 40 years in captivity.
